blocks.text: Fifth, if חולד choled is the mole, then חולד choled and עכבר achbar, that is, the mole and the mouse, are rightly joined in Moses, since the mole is akin to the mouse, and indeed a species of mouse, if we believe the Arabs; and Hesychius, for whom Λὼτ [Lōt] is ἀσπάλαξ [aspalax], the mole, or μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn], a blind mouse that bores through the earth; and the Scholiast on Aristophanes in the Acharnians, where he defines σκάλοπας [skalopas] as μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας [myas tinas, hous phamen spalakas], certain mice, which we call moles; and Oecumenius on 2 Petri I, 9., where he holds that μυωπάζειν [myōpazein] is the same as τυφλώττειν [typhlōttein], to be blind, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπὸ τὴν γῆν μυῶν τυφλῶν εἰς ἅπαν διατελούντων [apo tōn hypo tēn gēn myōn typhlōn eis hapan diatelountōn], from the mice which live under the earth entirely blind, [II, 440] that is, from moles. Accordingly, according to Scaliger ^{b)}, the mole belongs to the genus of mice. For others the mole is merely an animal similar to the mouse. Suidas: Ἔστι δὲ ὁ ἀσπάλαξ ζῶον μυῒ ἐμφερὲς, ὑπὸ γῆν διάγον, τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ ἐστερημένον [Esti de ho aspalax zōon myi empheres, hypo gēn diagon, tō ophthalmō esterēmenon]; The mole is an animal similar to the mouse, living under the earth, deprived of eyes. Accordingly they are joined in the passage of the Talmud [col. 1025] that we cited, צדין אישות ועכברים, They hunt moles and mice. But the weasel is a quite different animal, larger and stronger than the mouse, and as hostile to it as the cat. Hence Theophrastus, in the little book On the animals that appear in multitudes [?], in the passage where he treats of mice: Φθείρουσι δ' αὐτοὺς καὶ αἱ ἄγριαι γαλαῖ [Phtheirousi d' autous kai hai agriai galai]; Wild weasels kill them. And the author of the Batrachomyomachia, whoever he is, line 9[?]:
Μῦς ποτε διψαλέος, γαλέης κίνδυνον ἀλύξας, [Mys pote dipsaleos, galeēs kindynon alyxas,]

A mouse once, thirsty, having escaped the danger of a weasel. And in Athenaeus the poet Carcinus wrote a play entitled Μῦες [Myes], in which a weasel strangles mice by night. Plautus too, in the Stichus, Act 3:
A weasel snatched a mouse away from right before my feet. It did its shopping briskly. — — —

Likewise Pliny, book 8, chapter 27: The weasel (restores its strength) with rue when hunting mice, once it has joined battle with them. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 3: The weasel also pursues serpents and mice. Abdollatif of Baghdad ^{(5)}: ربما عادي الفار وقتله لكن الخوف الفار من السنور اشد خوفه منه [rubbamā ʿādā al-fār wa-qatalahu lākin al-khawf al-fār min al-sinnawr ashadd khawfihi minhu] It (the weasel) sometimes pursues mice and kills them. Yet the mouse fears the cat more gravely than the weasel.

Sixth, the verb חלד chalad (from which חולד choled is derived) means to penetrate and to dig under. It is properly said of the earth, as these examples show. The Jerusalem Talmud, in Kilayim, last chapter, as the distinguished Buxtorf cites it: מחליד הקב״ה לפניהם את הארץ God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, digging under the earth before them. And the Babylonian Talmud, in Bava Batra fol. 19 b, of vines: מפני שמחלידין את הקרקע ומעלין עפר תיחוח Because they dig under the ground and loosen the soil. And the Syriac translator of the hedgehog in Es. XXXIV, 15.: ܘܢܚܠܕ ܘܢܥܘܠ ܒܛܠܠܗ And it will dig out, and penetrate into its shade. From this it is transferred metaphorically to other things. [II, 441] Thus חלד, of metals, is to contract rust; and חלודה, rust, in Jonathan חלדות, Num. XXXI, 22., because it penetrates metals and eats into them to their innermost parts. Likewise gangrene is called ܡܣܟܝܢܘܬܐ in the Syriac paraphrase, 2 Tim. II, 17., because it is a disease that is ὑπόνομος [hyponomos], penetrating deeper into the flesh. Again, in slaughtering a victim, חלדה was the name for the deep plunging of the knife into the victim, which rendered the slaughter illegitimate, as is found in the Talmudic tractate Chullin, ch. 2, fol. 20 b, and in Maimonides' treatise On Slaughtering, ch. 3, §§ 9 and 10. To the same belongs the fact that in 2 Tim. III, 6., for Paul's words οἱ ἐνδύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας [hoi endynontes eis tas oikias], that is, who penetrate into houses, the Syriac has ܕܡܣܟܝܢ ܒܒܝܬ ܒܬܐ. For it speaks there of those who, as if making for the depths of houses, search and scrutinize everything most hidden. Accordingly the Arabic version published at Paris rendered it with a not dissimilar metaphor: الذين يغوصون في المنازل [alladhīna yaghūṣūna fī al-manāzil] who plunge themselves into houses. Nor does the conjecture of the most learned Fuller, Miscellanies, book 3, chapter 14, lack plausibility: that the Chalybes near Trapezus and Pharnacia were called Chaldaeans by the Phoenicians not because they had anything in common with the Babylonian Chaldaeans, but as חלדיא, or καταδύτας [katadytas], because they searched the bowels of the earth to dig metals out of it. They are thought to have been the first of all to devote effort to this. Callimachus, in the elegy On the Lock of Berenice:
— — Χαλύβων ὡς ἀπόλοιτο γένος, [Chalybōn hōs apoloito genos,] [col. 1026] Γειόθεν ἀντέλλον τι κακὸν φυτὸν οἵ μιν ἔφηναν. [Geiothen antellon ti kakon phyton hoi min ephēnan.]
— — May the whole race of the Chalybes perish, And he who first began to seek veins beneath the earth, etc.
Valerius too, in book 5 of the Argonautica, says elegantly of the same people:
